RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Franks in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Lower Rhine & Toxandria, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Franks was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Lower Rhine & Toxandria, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Porters haul cart wheels out of sodden ruts while the paymaster counts out a handful of rye. Requisitioned grain has gone hard as granite, and a man paid in salt or copper counts himself lucky. Each soldier watches the baggage train for silver he might strip from fallen enemies, because the field offers no other return on his labor.

By candlelight, the estate steward balances his ledgers. Three forges produced two hundred horseshoes and eighty spearheads last month, and the surplus olive oil sold at the spring fair will fund the knights' armor. Tenant villages pay their tithe late, so he has promised the toll collectors a share of the river dues to keep the trade road open.
